---
title: "Before Units"
subtitle: "The primitive mathematics is dimensionless"
toc: true
---

Science measures almost everything with units.

Distance is measured in meters.

Time is measured in seconds.

Energy is measured in joules.

Force is measured in newtons.

Temperature is measured in kelvin.

But before any of those measurements can be made, something must already be
distinguishable enough to measure.

R<sup>2</sup>D begins there.

> **Science is not made of units.  
> Science uses units to read primitive counts.**

The primitive R<sup>2</sup>D architecture is therefore dimensionless.

Units come later.

## A Measurement Requires Something to Measure

Suppose we measure a distance.

Before assigning meters, two distinguishable positions must already exist.

Suppose we measure a recurrence rate.

Before assigning inverse seconds, some recurrence must already be countable.

Suppose we measure an energy difference.

Before assigning joules, distinguishable states and a relation between them
must already have been defined.

Thus the logical order cannot begin with the unit.

It must begin with the distinction.

Schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{count relation}
\rightarrow
\text{physical coordinate}
\rightarrow
\text{unit}.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D develops the first two steps before introducing the last two.

## Counting Is Dimensionless

A count does not require a physical unit.

If a macrostate has

$$
W_{n,i}=120
$$

compatible realizations, the number

$$
120
$$

is simply a count.

It is not

$$
120\ \mathrm{J},
$$

or

$$
120\ \mathrm{m},
$$

or

$$
120\ \mathrm{s}.
$$

Likewise, a ratio of counts is dimensionless.

For example,

$$
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
$$

has no physical unit.

And therefore its logarithm

$$
\ln
\left(
\frac{W_{n,k}}{W_{n,i}}
\right)
$$

is dimensionless as well.

This gives R<sup>2</sup>D a mathematical language before physical
dimensionalization.

## Multiplicity Comes Before Entropy Units

For macrostate $i$,

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D defines its logarithmic multiplicity coordinate as

$$
\boxed{
S_{n,i}
=
\ln W_{n,i}.
}
$$

At this stage,

$$
S_{n,i}
$$

is dimensionless.

It is not yet thermodynamic entropy in units such as

$$
\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.
$$

The primitive relation is simply

$$
\boxed{
W
\longleftrightarrow
\ln W.
}
$$

Thermodynamic dimensionalization comes later.

[Multiplicity →](multiplicity.qmd)

## Why the Logarithm Appears

Suppose compatible possibilities compose multiplicatively:

$$
W_{\mathrm{whole}}
=
\prod_\alpha W_\alpha.
$$

Taking the logarithm gives

$$
\boxed{
\ln W_{\mathrm{whole}}
=
\sum_\alpha
\ln W_\alpha.
}
$$

Thus multiplication of compatible possibilities becomes addition in
logarithmic coordinates.

This relationship exists before any physical unit is introduced.

The logarithm is not creating the multiplicity.

It is providing an additive coordinate for multiplicative count structure.

Conversely,

$$
\boxed{
W=e^S
}
$$

recovers the multiplicity from its logarithmic coordinate.

> **Multiplicity is primitive.  
> The logarithm is its additive reading.**

## Addition Can Hide Multiplication

Much of science is written in additive coordinates.

Energy differences add.

Entropy changes add.

Actions add.

Potentials add.

But R<sup>2</sup>D asks whether some of those additive structures are
physical readings of a deeper multiplicative count architecture.

At the primitive count level:

$$
\boxed{
\text{compatible possibilities multiply}
}
$$

while

$$
\boxed{
\text{mutually exclusive alternatives add}.
}
$$

Logarithms make multiplicative composition readable through addition.

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D begins beneath the physical units attached to the
additive coordinates.

## Dimensionless Does Not Mean Unphysical

Calling the primitive structure dimensionless does not mean calling it
abstract in the sense of physically irrelevant.

R<sup>2</sup>D makes a stronger proposal.

The dimensionless relation is the structure that exists **before a particular
physical coordinate system has been assigned to it**.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{dimensionless}
\neq
\text{physically meaningless}.
}
$$

Instead:

$$
\boxed{
\text{dimensionless}
=
\text{not yet assigned a domain-specific physical unit}.
}
$$

A later physical theory can provide that read.

## The Boundary Comes Before the Ruler

A boundary defines which differences count as distinctions.

Only after those distinctions are defined can a ruler be assigned.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinguishability}
\rightarrow
\text{physical ruler}.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D does not begin with a universal ruler and then ask what objects
fit inside it.

It begins with the count boundary and asks which physical coordinate makes
that relation readable in a particular domain.

[Scientific Objecthood →](scientific-objecthood.qmd)

## Distinguishability Is Not Yet Length

For a readable transition

$$
i\rightarrow k,
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D defines a distinguishable interval

$$
\lambda_{n,i\rightarrow k}.
$$

At the primitive level,

$$
\lambda
$$

is not necessarily a spatial displacement.

It records the readable distinguishable interval between states.

A later physical mapping might assign a spatial, mechanical, chemical, or
other physical coordinate to that distinction.

But Part I does not assume which one.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\lambda
\neq
\text{primitive length}.
}
$$

Length can be one physical read of distinguishability.

## Recurrence Is Not Yet Time

Likewise, R<sup>2</sup>D defines completed recurrence before introducing a
clock.

For adjacent boundaries,

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\chi_{n+1})
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha})
}.
$$

This is a ratio of completed recurrence counts.

It has no unit of seconds.

It has no unit of hertz.

It is dimensionless.

Only later can a physical system test whether this count relation can be
read as a ratio of physical rates.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{possible physical time or rate read}.
}
$$

Not:

$$
\text{time}
\rightarrow
\text{recurrence}.
$$

[Recurrence →](recurrence.qmd)

## Space and Time Therefore Come Later

This produces one of the stronger claims of Part I.

Boundaries, multiplicities, occurrences, occupancies, closures, and
recurrences can all be defined without assuming a pre-existing spacetime.

Therefore R<sup>2</sup>D does not place its count architecture inside a
primitive space-time container.

Instead, it asks whether spatial and temporal coordinates are later physical
readings of relations that have already been defined.

Schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\text{distinguishability}
\rightarrow
\text{spatial read}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{temporal or rate read}.
}
$$

These mappings are later physical hypotheses.

They are not assumptions required to construct Part I.

## R<sup>2</sup>D Does Not Reject Continuous Mathematics

Beginning from discrete count does not mean rejecting calculus or continuous
coordinates.

A continuous coordinate can provide an extremely accurate representation of
large numbers of unresolved count relations.

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore distinguishes:

$$
\boxed{
\text{primitive count structure}
}
$$

from

$$
\boxed{
\text{continuous physical representation}.
}
$$

The success of calculus does not require the primitive ontology itself to
begin as a continuously divisible coordinate system.

Continuous mathematics can remain an exact or extraordinarily accurate read
of recursively organized count.

## Physical Coordinates Can Compress Count Structure

Imagine a very large number of small distinguishable changes.

Resolving every individual count may be unnecessary or impossible.

A smooth coordinate can represent their collective relation.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{many unresolved count relations}
\rightarrow
\text{continuous readable coordinate}.
}
$$

This does not make the continuous description false.

It identifies the logical level at which it appears.

The physical coordinate is a representation of already-organized
distinguishability.

## Probability Also Comes Later

Probability offers another example.

Multiplicity is possible count:

$$
W_{n,i}.
$$

A probability can be formed only after a total count domain has been chosen.

For example,

$$
\boxed{
p_{n,i}
=
\frac{
W_{n,i}
}{
\sum_j W_{n,j}
}.
}
$$

The normalization does not create the possible states.

It reads their relative multiplicities fractionally.

Likewise, an observed occupancy fraction might be

$$
p_{n,i}^{\mathrm{obs}}
=
\frac{
c_{n,i}
}{
\sum_j c_{n,j}
}.
$$

Again, the probability is constructed after the count structure exists.

Thus:

> **Possible count comes before probability.**

[Occupancy and Occurrence →](occupancy-occurrence.qmd)

## Probability Is Not Possibility

R<sup>2</sup>D possibility is

$$
P_{n,i}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
\Theta_{n+1|n,i}
}{
W_{n,i}
}
\right).
$$

This measures compatible enclosing extension.

Probability is a normalized reading of count.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
P
\neq
p.
}
$$

Possibility belongs to the recursive count architecture.

Probability appears only after a count domain is normalized.

This distinction is important because R<sup>2</sup>D does not need
probability to define direction.

[Possibility →](possibility.qmd)

## Energy Also Comes Later

The same logic applies to energy.

Before assigning an energy difference to two states, the states themselves
must already be distinguishable.

Thus the logical order is

$$
\boxed{
\text{state distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{count relation}
\rightarrow
\text{energetic read}.
}
$$

R<sup>2</sup>D does not deny energy.

It places energy downstream of a dimensionless state architecture.

In Part II, thermodynamics supplies some of the strongest physical
calibrations of this idea.

But the primitive count relation exists before the energetic units are
attached.

## Force Also Comes Later

The local retention relation is

$$
\Delta R
=
C^{\mathrm{out}}\lambda.
$$

Neither

$$
C
$$

nor

$$
\lambda
$$

is primitively mechanical.

In a mechanical system, a physical mapping may make the product resemble a
familiar force-displacement relation.

But that physical interpretation comes after the abstract relation has been
defined.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
C
\neq
\text{primitive force}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\lambda
\neq
\text{primitive displacement}.
}
$$

[Constraint and Retention →](constraint-retention.qmd)

## The R<sup>2</sup>D Law Is Dimensionless First

The R<sup>2</sup>D law is

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
C_{n+1}
\lambda_{n+1}
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}.
}
$$

Every quantity is defined as part of the dimensionless count architecture.

No joules are required.

No meters are required.

No seconds are required.

No kelvin are required.

This is deliberate.

Only after a physical domain supplies appropriate mappings can the equation
acquire familiar unit-bearing coordinates.

[The R²D Law →](r2d-law.qmd)

## Dimensionalization Is a Physical Mapping

The general logic is

$$
\boxed{
\text{dimensionless count relation}
\rightarrow
\text{domain-specific physical read}.
}
$$

For example, a domain may provide a physical read of:

$$
S
$$

as an entropy coordinate,

$$
\lambda
$$

as a spatial or mechanical distinction,

$$
\rho
$$

as a rate relation,

or

$$
C\lambda
$$

as a constrained physical quantity.

But those mappings must be established.

They cannot simply be assumed because the symbols resemble familiar physical
variables.

## The Mapping Must Preserve the Count Relation

A valid physical dimensionalization must preserve the underlying structure.

If two physical quantities are proposed as reads of two R<sup>2</sup>D
coordinates, their measured relation must reproduce the primitive count
relation.

This gives the mapping empirical content.

The procedure is not:

$$
\text{choose familiar equation}
\rightarrow
\text{rename its terms R²D}.
$$

It is:

$$
\boxed{
\text{define count relation}
\rightarrow
\text{identify physical reads}
\rightarrow
\text{test the mapping}.
}
$$

That order is fundamental to the R<sup>2</sup>D program.

## Physical Constants Can Enter at the Mapping

A dimensionless relation and a dimensional physical relation cannot be
identified without a calibration.

Physical constants can participate in that calibration.

For example, conventional thermodynamics relates logarithmic multiplicity to
unit-bearing entropy through a dimensional factor.

R<sup>2</sup>D separates the two levels:

$$
\boxed{
\ln W
}
$$

is the primitive count coordinate,

while the physically calibrated thermodynamic quantity appears only after
the relevant dimensional mapping is supplied.

The constant belongs to the physical read.

The count comes first.

## Units Are Boundary-Specific Reads

Different scientific boundaries can assign different physical meanings to
the same primitive type of count relation.

A distinguishability relation might receive one physical read in mechanics
and another in chemistry.

A recurrence relation might receive one read in spectroscopy and another in
biological kinetics.

The primitive grammar does not require the units to be identical.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{common count architecture}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{common physical unit}.
}
$$

This is a central reason R<sup>2</sup>D can compare different scientific
domains without forcing them into one pre-existing coordinate system.

## Different Units Can Describe Different Readability Regimes

The physical vocabulary appropriate to a system depends on what remains
readable from the relevant boundary.

One domain may make recurrence especially accessible.

Another may make geometric distinguishability especially accessible.

Another may allow both to be jointly read.

The physical units and variables can therefore differ dramatically even
when the underlying count grammar is related.

This is the basis for the later R<sup>2</sup>D readability program.

## Unification Before Units

This changes the meaning of scientific unification.

A conventional unification program often attempts to reconcile quantities
that already carry physical meanings:

- mass;
- charge;
- energy;
- field;
- spacetime;
- curvature;
- frequency.

R<sup>2</sup>D asks whether that begins too late.

Once those quantities have units, much of the boundary-specific projection
has already occurred.

The proposed common structure may lie beneath them.

Thus:

> **R<sup>2</sup>D does not first try to put every science into one unit
> system.**

> **It asks whether they share one dimensionless count grammar before their
> units diverge.**

This is **unification before units**.

## Unification Does Not Mean One Universal Ruler

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore does not require one primitive spatial ruler.

It does not require one primitive energetic coordinate.

It does not require one universal clock already present beneath every
scientific domain.

The proposed invariant is earlier:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{multiplicity}
\rightarrow
\text{realization}
\rightarrow
\text{closure}
\rightarrow
\text{recurrence}.
}
$$

Physical rulers are assigned afterward.

## Why This Matters for Scientific Objecthood

This connects directly to boundary-relative objects.

An object must be distinguishable before physical properties can be assigned
to it.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{objecthood}
\rightarrow
\text{physical measurement}.
}
$$

The meter does not create the object.

The joule does not create the state.

The second does not create the recurrence.

The probability does not create the possible count.

The units tell us how an already-defined relation is physically readable.

[Scientific Objecthood →](scientific-objecthood.qmd)

## The Primitive Mathematics Is the Common Layer

By this stage, R<sup>2</sup>D has defined without physical units:

$$
B_n
$$

for the count boundary,

$$
W_{n,i}
$$

for multiplicity,

$$
S_{n,i}
=
\ln W_{n,i}
$$

for logarithmic multiplicity,

$$
\nu_{n,i}
$$

for occurrence count,

$$
c_{n,i}
$$

for occupancy,

$$
P_{n,i}
$$

for compatible enclosing possibility,

$$
C_{n+1}
$$

for enclosing constraint,

$$
\lambda_n
$$

for distinguishability,

$$
\mathcal C_n
$$

for closure,

and

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}
$$

for relative recurrence.

The physical sciences can then ask how these relations become readable
through their own coordinates.

## What Part I Does — and Does Not — Establish

Part I establishes the dimensionless architecture.

It does **not** automatically establish every proposed physical mapping.

It does not prove merely from notation that

$$
\lambda
$$

must be physical length,

that

$$
\rho
$$

must be physical frequency,

or that any particular physical energy must equal a chosen count coordinate.

Those are mapping questions.

They require empirical and mathematical justification in the later program.

This distinction protects the direction of the argument:

> **First define the mathematics.  
> Then test how physics reads it.**

## The Architecture in One View

The R<sup>2</sup>D ordering can be summarized as

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c}
\text{boundary}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{distinguishable states}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{dimensionless multiplicity}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{occurrence and occupancy}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{closure and recurrence}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{recursive count relation}
\\[8pt]
\Downarrow
\\[8pt]
\text{physical dimensionalization}
\\[4pt]
\Downarrow
\\[4pt]
\text{meters, seconds, joules, kelvin, volts, pascals, \ldots}
\end{array}
}
$$

The unit-bearing world appears at the end of the sequence, not the beginning.

## The Key Distinction

The simplest summary is:

> **A unit measures a relation.  
> It does not create the relation being measured.**

> **A physical coordinate makes recursive count readable in a particular
> domain.  
> It does not have to be primitive to that count.**

> **R<sup>2</sup>D therefore defines the common mathematics before assigning
> the units through which different sciences read it.**

Or, more compactly:

> **Science uses units to read primitive counts.  
> R<sup>2</sup>D begins before units are assigned.**

The next step is to ask how this dimensionless count architecture acquires
the familiar physical quantities used by science.
